claim: TFEB and TFE3 belong to the MiTF-TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) transcription factors.
source: TFEB and TFE3 belong to the MiTF-TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) transcription factors and have been well characterized as master regulators of the autophagy-lysosome pathway in response to starvation (Martina et al., 2014; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Martina et al., 2014; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011) that characterize TFEB and TFE3.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 are master regulators of the autophagy-lysosome pathway in response to starvation.
source: TFEB and TFE3 belong to the MiTF-TFE family of basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ) transcription factors and have been well characterized as master regulators of the autophagy-lysosome pathway in response to starvation (Martina et al., 2014; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Martina et al., 2014; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011) establishing this regulatory role.

claim: Under nutrient poor conditions, TFEB and TFE3 translocate to the nucleus where they bind to CLEAR elements in the promoters of autophagic and lysosomal genes.
source: Under nutrient poor conditions, TFEB and TFE3 translocate to the nucleus where they bind to and promote transcription from consensus 10 bp GTCACGTGAC sequences, termed Coordinated Lysosome Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) elements, in the promoters of autophagic and lysosomal genes, (Martina et al., 2014; Palmieri et al., 2011; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Martina et al., 2014; Palmieri et al., 2011; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011) that describe this mechanism.

claim: CLEAR elements are consensus 10 bp GTCACGTGAC sequences.
source: Under nutrient poor conditions, TFEB and TFE3 translocate to the nucleus where they bind to and promote transcription from consensus 10 bp GTCACGTGAC sequences, termed Coordinated Lysosome Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) elements, in the promoters of autophagic and lysosomal genes, (Martina et al., 2014; Palmieri et al., 2011; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations defining CLEAR elements (Martina et al., 2014; Palmieri et al., 2011; Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011).

claim: Under adequate nutrient conditions, TFEB and TFE3 bind to Rag GTPases on the lysosome surface.
source: Under conditions of adequate nutrient status, TFEB and TFE3 bind to a pair of heterodimeric small GTPases, termed RagA or RagB (RagA/B) and RagC or RagD (RagC/D) on the lysosome surface (Martina and Puertollano, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Martina and Puertollano, 2013) describing this interaction.

claim: Rag GTPases recruit mTORC1, which phosphorylates TFEB at Ser211 and TFE3 at Ser321.
source: These Rag GTPases also recruit the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1), which phosphorylates TFEB at Ser211 and TFE3 at Ser321, thus creating a binding site for proteins in the 14-3-3 family which sequester TFEB and TFE3 in the cytosol by masking their nuclear localization signals (Martina et al., 2012; Martina et al., 2014; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Martina et al., 2012; Martina et al., 2014; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012) describing this phosphorylation mechanism.

claim: Phosphorylation of TFEB and TFE3 by mTORC1 creates a binding site for 14-3-3 proteins which sequester TFEB and TFE3 in the cytosol.
source: These Rag GTPases also recruit the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1), which phosphorylates TFEB at Ser211 and TFE3 at Ser321, thus creating a binding site for proteins in the 14-3-3 family which sequester TFEB and TFE3 in the cytosol by masking their nuclear localization signals (Martina et al., 2012; Martina et al., 2014; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Martina et al., 2012; Martina et al., 2014; Powis and De Virgilio, 2016; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012) describing the sequestration mechanism.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 are activated by inflammatory or pathogenic signals, ER stress, oxidative stress, and high intensity exercise.
source: Recently, other cellular stressors such as inflammatory or pathogenic signals, ER stress, oxidative stress, and high intensity exercise have been implicated in activating TFEB and TFE3 via a variety of mechanisms involving mTORC1 as well as other kinases and phosphatases, including calcineurin and PP2A (Chen et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Martina et al., 2016; Martina and Puertollano, 2018; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Chen et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Martina et al., 2016; Martina and Puertollano, 2018; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Visvikis et al., 2014) describing activation by various stressors.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 activation by various stressors involves mTORC1 as well as other kinases and phosphatases, including calcineurin and PP2A.
source: Recently, other cellular stressors such as inflammatory or pathogenic signals, ER stress, oxidative stress, and high intensity exercise have been implicated in activating TFEB and TFE3 via a variety of mechanisms involving mTORC1 as well as other kinases and phosphatases, including calcineurin and PP2A (Chen et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Martina et al., 2016; Martina and Puertollano, 2018; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Chen et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Martina et al., 2016; Martina and Puertollano, 2018; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Visvikis et al., 2014) describing the mechanisms.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 exhibit cell or tissue type specific responses including pro-inflammatory, chemoattractant, and antimicrobial responses in immune cells.
source: In addition to being regulated by multiple physiological stressors, TFEB and TFE3 exhibit unique cell or tissue type specific responses including pro-inflammatory, chemoattractant, and antimicrobial responses in immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells; lipid metabolism in liver and adipose tissue; and mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014) describing cell-type specific responses.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 regulate lipid metabolism in liver and adipose tissue.
source: In addition to being regulated by multiple physiological stressors, TFEB and TFE3 exhibit unique cell or tissue type specific responses including pro-inflammatory, chemoattractant, and antimicrobial responses in immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells; lipid metabolism in liver and adipose tissue; and mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014) describing tissue-specific functions.

claim: TFEB and TFE3 regulate mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle.
source: In addition to being regulated by multiple physiological stressors, TFEB and TFE3 exhibit unique cell or tissue type specific responses including pro-inflammatory, chemoattractant, and antimicrobial responses in immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells; lipid metabolism in liver and adipose tissue; and mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bretou et al., 2017; Mansueto et al., 2017; Najibi et al., 2016; Pastore et al., 2016; Settembre et al., 2013; Visvikis et al., 2014) describing muscle-specific functions.

claim: p53 integrates DNA damage signals resulting in transcriptional programs governing cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence, and apoptosis.
source: The tumor suppressor transcription factor p53 integrates DNA damage signals resulting in transcriptional programs governing the diverse processes of the DNA damage response (DDR) including cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence, and when the stress is severe enough, apoptosis (Bieging and Attardi, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Bieging and Attardi, 2012) describing p53's role in DNA damage response.

claim: p53 responds to multiple cellular stressors including nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and hypoxia.
source: Much like TFE3 and TFEB, p53 has been shown to respond to multiple cellular stressors including nutrient deprivation, oxidative stress, and hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about p53's response to various stressors.

claim: p53 has roles controlling transcriptional activity towards autophagy, cell migration, and metabolism.
source: Similarly, p53 has roles controlling transcriptional activity towards processes not canonically associated with the DDR, including autophagy, cell migration, and metabolism (Bieging and Attardi, 2012; Nishida et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Bieging and Attardi, 2012; Nishida et al., 2016) describing p53's non-canonical roles.

claim: p53 activity is controlled through posttranslational modifications at approximately 50 residues.
source: p53 activity is controlled through an extensive repertoire of posttranslational modifications at approximately 50 residues which include phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, ubiquitylation, sumoylation, and poly-ADP-ribosylation (Meek and Anderson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Meek and Anderson, 2009) describing p53 posttranslational modifications.

claim: Under baseline conditions, p53 is rapidly ubiquitylated and degraded by the E3 ligase Mdm2.
source: Under baseline conditions, p53 is rapidly ubiquitylated and degraded by the E3 ligase, Mdm2, limiting its activity.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge about p53 regulation by Mdm2.

claim: In response to DNA damage, p53 is rapidly phosphorylated and acetylated by kinases and acetyltransferases.
source: In response to DNA damage and other stressors, p53 is rapidly phosphorylated and acetylated by a large variety of kinases and acetyltransferases which serve to stabilize and modulate binding to p53 response elements in the promoters of different classes of genes (Meek and Anderson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Meek and Anderson, 2009) describing p53 modifications in response to DNA damage.

claim: p53 has a suppressive function on autophagy attributed to its cytosolic form.
source: Importantly, p53 has critical and multifaceted roles in regulating autophagy, including a suppressive function attributed to its cytosolic form and a more well-established pro-autophagic function owing to its transcriptional activity in the nucleus (Kenzelmann Broz et al., 2013; Tasdemir et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Kenzelmann Broz et al., 2013; Tasdemir et al., 2008) describing p53's suppressive role in autophagy.

claim: p53 has a pro-autophagic function owing to its transcriptional activity in the nucleus.
source: Importantly, p53 has critical and multifaceted roles in regulating autophagy, including a suppressive function attributed to its cytosolic form and a more well-established pro-autophagic function owing to its transcriptional activity in the nucleus (Kenzelmann Broz et al., 2013; Tasdemir et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Kenzelmann Broz et al., 2013; Tasdemir et al., 2008) describing p53's pro-autophagic role.

claim: An alternative Atg5 and LC3-independent form of autophagy is induced in mouse embryonic fibroblasts in response to etoposide.
source: For example, an alternative Atg5 and LC3-independent form of autophagy is induced in mouse embryonic fibroblasts in response to the DNA damaging drug, etoposide (Nishida et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Nishida et al., 2009) describing this alternative autophagy pathway.

claim: Approximately half of all human cancers exhibit mutations at the TP53 locus.
source: The role of p53 in cancer has been studied extensively, with approximately half of all human cancers exhibiting mutations at the TP53 locus, while cancers without p53 mutations frequently have other alterations in the p53 pathway (Eliopoulos et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Eliopoulos et al., 2016) describing p53 mutations in cancer.

claim: TFE3 and TFEB gene fusions are detected in subsets of renal cell carcinomas.
source: While not as widely associated with all cancers, TFE3 and TFEB gene fusions are detected in subsets of renal cell carcinomas (RCC), indicating roles for these transcription factors in oncogenesis (Kauffman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation (Kauffman et al., 2014) describing TFE3 and TFEB gene fusions in RCC.

claim: Wild type MEFs exposed to etoposide show a time-dependent increase in TFE3 nuclear levels, with noticeable accumulation by 4 hr treatment.
source: We observed a time-dependent increase in the levels of TFE3 in the nucleus relative to the cytosol, with noticeable accumulation appearing by 4 hr treatment, and increasing amounts at 8 hr and 16 hr (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating TFE3 nuclear translocation over time.

claim: After 8 hr etoposide treatment, the nuclear localization of TFE3 is statistically significant compared to control.
source: After 8 hr treatment, the nuclear localization of TFE3 is statistically significant compared to control (Figure 1B; numerical values Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Cisplatin treatment induces TFE3 nuclear translocation in MEFs.
source: Despite this mechanistic difference in mode of DNA damage, cisplatin treatment also effectively induced TFE3 nuclear translocation in MEFs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating TFE3 translocation after cisplatin treatment.

claim: Ultraviolet light treatment induces TFE3 activation in MEFs.
source: Treatment with ultraviolet light, which primarily damages DNA through the formation of pyrimidine dimers (Gentile, 2003), also induced TFE3 activation in MEFs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and a citation (Gentile, 2003) describing UV-induced DNA damage.

claim: TFE3 nuclear accumulation in response to genotoxic stress is observed in ARPE-19, HeLa and RAW 264.7 cells.
source: We also confirmed that TFE3 nuclear accumulation in response to genotoxic stress was observed in other cell types, including ARPE-19, HeLa and RAW 264.7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C demonstrating TFE3 translocation in multiple cell types.

claim: Subcellular fractionation experiments show a significant increase in nuclear TFE3 and TFEB following DNA damage.
source: Finally, we performed subcellular fractionation experiments following treatment with either etoposide or cisplatin. As seen in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, we observed a significant increase in the amount of nuclear TFE3 and TFEB following DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H demonstrating nuclear accumulation by fractionation.

claim: Treatment with DNA damaging agents results in a time dependent decrease in TFE3 S321 phosphorylation.
source: Activation of TFE3 requires dephosphorylation of serine 321. Treatment of several cell types with different DNA damaging agents, resulted in a time dependent decrease in S321 phosphorylation that correlated with the degree of TFE3 nuclear translocation observed by immunofluorescence (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G demonstrating dephosphorylation.

claim: TFEB exhibits a pronounced gel-shift following DNA damage, indicative of dephosphorylation.
source: TFEB serine 211 (S211) is the equivalent residue to TFE3 S321, however phospho-specific antibodies generated against this residue are not detectable with endogenous TFEB levels. Nonetheless, TFEB exhibits a pronounced gel-shift following DNA damage, which is indicative of dephosphorylation, thus suggesting a similar regulation of both transcription factors in response to DNA damage (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G demonstrating TFEB gel-shift.

claim: Treatment of HeLa cells stably expressing TFEB-FLAG with UV-C light results in rapid dephosphorylation of TFE3 and TFEB at S321 and S211.
source: Furthermore, treatment of a HeLa clone that stably expresses TFEB-FLAG with UV-C light resulted in a rapid dephosphorylation of TFE3 and TFEB at S321 and S211, respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F demonstrating dephosphorylation after UV-C treatment.

claim: Etoposide treatment results in a time-dependent decrease in S6K and 4EBP1 phosphorylation levels.
source: Treatment with etoposide also resulted in a time-dependent decrease in S6K and 4EBP1 phosphorylation levels that mirrors the kinetics of observed TFE3 nuclear translocation, suggesting that mTORC1 inhibition may be a major mechanism by which DNA damage promotes TFE3 and TFEB activation (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G demonstrating mTORC1 inhibition.

claim: The degree of mTORC1 inhibition after 8 hr etoposide is not as potent as that induced by starvation.
source: It is notable that the degree of mTORC1 inhibition after 8 hr etoposide was not as potent as that induced by starvation and closely correlates with the degree of dephosphorylation and nuclear redistribution of TFE3 under etoposide treated and starvation conditions, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from comparing experimental data on mTORC1 inhibition under different conditions.

claim: DNA damage reduces mTORC1 activity in ARPE-19 cells.
source: The effect of DNA damage on reducing mTORC1 activity was also observed in ARPE-19 cells, which could tolerate extended etoposide treatment past 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), as well as in HeLa cells treated with UVC (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I and Figure 1F demonstrating mTORC1 inhibition in ARPE-19 and HeLa cells.

claim: Activation of the DNA damage response leads to p53-dependent mTORC1 inactivation.
source: Several studies have reported that the activation of the DNA damage response (DDR) leads to p53-dependent mTORC1 inactivation (Budanov and Karin, 2008; Cam et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Budanov and Karin, 2008; Cam et al., 2014; Feng et al., 2005) describing p53-dependent mTORC1 inactivation.

claim: Etoposide treatment results in a time-dependent decrease in mTORC1 activity in WT MEFs but not in p53-/- MEFs.
source: As predicted, etoposide treatment resulted in a time-dependent decrease in mTORC1 activity in WT MEFs, whereas this decrease was virtually absent in p53-/- MEFs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A comparing mTORC1 activity in WT and p53-/- MEFs.

claim: p53-/- MEFs display a strong reduction in mTORC1 signaling in response to starvation.
source: Unlike with DNA damage, p53-/- MEFs still displayed a strong reduction in mTORC1 signaling in response to starvation, although the levels remained slightly elevated when compared with WT MEFs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating mTORC1 inhibition by starvation in p53-/- MEFs.

claim: There is a significantly reduced proportion of cells with TFE3 in the nucleus in p53-/- compared to WT MEFs after etoposide treatment.
source: TFE3 localization, as assessed by immunofluorescence, revealed a significantly reduced proportion of cells with TFE3 in the nucleus in p53-/- compared to WT MEFs (Figure 2C and D; numerical values Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the number of cells showing TFEB nuclear accumulation in etoposide-treated p53-/- MEFs.
source: Similar results were obtained when analyzing TFEB distribution, with a significant reduction in the number of cells showing TFEB nuclear accumulation in etoposide-treated p53-/- MEFs (Figure 2E and F; numerical values Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F with statistical analysis.

claim: Western blots of lysates from WT MEFs treated with etoposide reveal prominent gel shifts in TFE3 and TFEB, which are absent in etoposide treated p53-/- MEFs.
source: Moreover, western blots of lysates from WT MEFs treated with etoposide revealed prominent gel shifts in TFE3 and TFEB, which were absent in etoposide treated p53-/- MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A demonstrating gel shifts.

claim: Expression of active Rags prevents translocation of endogenous TFE3 to the nucleus following etoposide treatment.
source: As expected, expression of active Rags, and consequent constitutive mTORC1 activation, prevented translocation of endogenous TFE3 to the nucleus following etoposide treatment (Figure 2G and H; numerical values Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H demonstrating that active Rags prevent TFE3 translocation.

claim: mTORC1 inactivation is required for TFE3 activation in response to DNA damage.
source: These data corroborate that mTORC1 inactivation is required for TFE3 activation in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that constitutive mTORC1 activation prevents TFE3 translocation.

claim: There is a statistically significant reduction in the nuclear TFE3 population in p53-/- MEFs exposed to starvation conditions.
source: We also observed a statistically significant reduction in the nuclear TFE3 population in p53-/- MEFs exposed to starvation conditions, suggesting that p53 may play an unexpected role in the regulation of the starvation response with regards to regulation of TFE3 and TFEB (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of Lamp1, Mcoln1, Atp6vc1, and Ctsd is significantly reduced in p53-/- MEFs under starvation.
source: Accordingly, transcriptional upregulation of several TFEB and TFE3 targets, including Lamp1, Mcoln1, Atp6vc1, and Ctsd, was significantly reduced in p53-/- MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; numerical values Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B demonstrating reduced gene expression.

claim: Treatment of WT MEFs with etoposide induces upregulation of p53 regulated DDR genes including Cdkn1a, Mdm2, Trp53inp1.
source: Treatment of WT MEFs induced a potent upregulation of typical p53 regulated DDR genes involved in cell cycle arrest, autophagy, and apoptosis. These included Cdkn1a, Mdm2, Trp53inp1, and many others, confirming that our control cell line behaves in an appropriate manner in response to DNA damage insults (Figure 3; numerical values Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating gene upregulation.

claim: TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs exhibit large-scale dysregulation of the DDR with numerous p53-regulated transcripts significantly downregulated after etoposide exposure.
source: In contrast to the WT MEFs, TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs exhibited a large-scale dysregulation of the DDR, with numerous p53-regulated and p53 regulating transcripts significantly downregulated after exposure to etoposide, including, Rad9a, Chek2, Bbc3, Bax, Trp53inp1, Dram1, Mdm2, Sesn1, and Sesn2, among others (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 demonstrating gene dysregulation.

claim: Rad9a and Chek2 levels are strongly and significantly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs in response to etoposide treatment.
source: The levels of both Rad9a and Chek2 were strongly and significantly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs in response to etoposide treatment.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from RNA-Seq and qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Basal levels of Trp53inp1 and Mdm2 are strongly reduced in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs under etoposide treated conditions.
source: The basal levels of Trp53inp1 and Mdm2 were also strongly reduced in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs under etoposide treated conditions, indicating a novel role for TFE3 and TFEB in promoting their transcription in response to DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating reduced gene expression in DKO cells.

claim: Pro-apoptotic p53 transcribed genes Bbc3 and Bax are significantly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs under etoposide treated conditions.
source: Similarly, the pro-apoptotic p53 transcribed genes Bbc3 and Bax are significantly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs under etoposide treated conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating reduced gene expression in DKO cells.

claim: Both basal levels and etoposide induced levels of Dram1 mRNA are strongly reduced in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs.
source: We found that both basal levels and etoposide induced levels of Dram1 mRNA are strongly reduced in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data demonstrating reduced Dram1 expression in DKO cells.

claim: Sesn1 and Sesn2 are direct transcriptional targets of p53.
source: Sesn1 and Sesn2 are highly homologous stress responsive genes that inhibit mTORC1 activity (Cam et al., 2014). They are also both direct transcriptional targets of p53, thus providing a direct mechanistic link between p53 activation in response to DNA damage and TFE3 and TFEB activation (Budanov and Karin, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations (Cam et al., 2014; Budanov and Karin, 2008) describing Sesn1 and Sesn2 as p53 targets.

claim: Sesn1 and Sesn2 were among the strongest downregulated targets in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs in RNA-Seq experiments.
source: Sesn1 and Sesn2 were among the strongest downregulated targets in TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs in our RNA-Seq experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental RNA-Seq data.

claim: Etoposide induced expression of numerous DDR response genes is strongly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO RAW264.7 macrophages.
source: Indeed, the etoposide induced expression of numerous DDR response genes, including Bbc3, Trp53inp1, Sesn1, Sesn2, Chek2, Rad9a, Foxo3, Mdm2, and Wrap53 were strongly downregulated in TFEB/TFE3 DKO RAW264.7 macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; numerical values Figure 3-figure supplement 1-source data 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 demonstrating gene downregulation in RAW264.7 cells.

claim: WT RAW264.7 cells exhibit a rapid and sustained increase in total p53 levels and phosphorylation at serine 15 after etoposide treatment.
source: As expected, WT RAW264.7 exhibited a rapid and sustained increase in total p53 levels and levels of phosphorylation at serine 15.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis.

claim: TFEB/TFE3 DKO RAW264.7 cells show a rapid induction of total and phospho-serine 15 p53 until 2 hr etoposide treatment, after which levels decline.
source: Like the WT cells, TFEB/TFE3 DKO RAW264.7 showed a rapid induction of total and phospho-serine 15 p53 until 2 hr etoposide treatment. At this point, total and phospho-serine 15 p53 levels declined at a steady state until they reached close to baseline levels by 8 hr etoposide treatment (Figure 4A and B; numerical values Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B demonstrating p53 dynamics in DKO cells.

claim: Mdm2 levels are significantly higher in TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells at 2 and 4 hr etoposide treatment.
source: Furthermore, the levels of Mdm2 were significantly higher in the TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells at 2 and 4 hr etoposide treatment, precisely when the levels of p53 begin to diverge between the two genotypes (Figure 4A and C; numerical values Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and C with statistical analysis.

claim: p53 protein levels are elevated for a longer time in WT compared to DKO RAW264.7 cells after etoposide treatment.
source: As seen in Figure 4D and E; numerical values Figure 4—source data 3, p53 protein levels were elevated for a longer time in WT compared to DKO cells, consistent with our hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cycloheximide chase assay shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Nutlin-3 treatment drastically increases the levels of p53 in RAW264.7 TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells after 8 hr etoposide treatment.
source: In contrast, nutlin-3 drastically increased the levels of p53 in RAW264.7 TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells, bringing its levels on par with those observed in WT cells (Figure 4F and G; numerical values Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G demonstrating p53 rescue by nutlin-3.

claim: Overexpression of TFEB-S211A and TFE3-S321A dramatically increases basal p53 levels in HeLa cells.
source: Overexpression of the constitutively active forms of TFEB (TFEB-S211A) and TFE3 (TFE3-S321A) dramatically increased the basal levels of p53 observed in whole cell lysates (Figure 5A and B; numerical values Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B demonstrating increased p53 levels.

claim: Expression of TFEB-S211A and TFE3-S321A leads to a near uniform pattern of p53 expression, predominantly localized in the nuclei of HeLa cells.
source: However, expression of TFEB-S211A and TFE3-S321A led to a near uniform pattern of p53 expression, predominantly localized in the nuclei of HeLa cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating p53 nuclear localization.

claim: The half-life of endogenous p53 is extended beyond 60 min in TFEB-S211A expressing HeLa cells and 30 min in TFE3-S321A expressing cells.
source: The half-life of endogenous p53 is less than 15 min in HeLa cells under basal conditions. This was extended beyond 60 min in TFEB-S211A expressing cells and 30 min in TFE3-S321A expressing cells (Figure 5D and E; numerical values Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cycloheximide chase assay shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: TFEB nuclear localization is required for p53 stabilization.
source: This indicates that TFEB nuclear localization is required for p53 stabilization and this effect is therefore likely due to TFEB transcriptional activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing TFEB-S211A and TFEB-S211A/NLSmut effects on p53.

claim: Adenovirus mediated expression of TFEB-S211A and TFE3-S321A in HeLa cells leads to significantly increased expression of Bbc3, Trp53inp1, Sesn1, UVRAG and Rad9A.
source: Adenovirus mediated expression of TFEB-S211A and TFE3-S321A in HeLa cells lead to a significantly increased expression of the basal levels of a number of these genes, including Bbc3, Trp53inp1, Sesn1, UVRAG and Rad9A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C; numerical values Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Over-expression of TFEB-S211A and S321A does not cause Tp53 transcriptional upregulation.
source: Importantly, over-expression of TFEB-S211A and S321A did not cause Tp53 transcriptional upregulation, further suggesting a role of TFEB and TFE3 in promoting p53 protein stabilization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Etoposide treatment results in a time dependent increase in LMP in WT MEFs, with most cells exhibiting significant LMP by 8 hr.
source: In WT MEFs, etoposide treatment resulted in a time dependent increase in LMP, with most cells exhibiting significant LMP by 8 hr, while untreated MEFs exhibit extremely low levels of detectable LMP (Figure 6A–D; numerical values Figure 6—source datas 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–D demonstrating LMP induction.

claim: A significantly reduced proportion of TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs exhibit LMP by 8 hr etoposide treatment.
source: In TFEB/TFE3 DKO MEFs, a significantly reduced proportion of cells exhibit LMP by 8 hr etoposide, and those that do, had fewer galectin-1 positive puncta on average than control cells (Figure 6A and Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, C, and D with statistical analysis.

claim: LLOMe treated MEFs exhibit extensive and equivalent degrees of LMP activity in both WT and DKO backgrounds.
source: In contrast to etoposide treatment, LLOMe treated MEFs exhibited extensive and equivalent degrees of LMP activity in both WT and DKO backgrounds (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating LMP induction by LLOMe.

claim: WT RAW264.7 cells exhibit a sustained and much higher degree of detectable Caspase-3 cleavage after prolonged etoposide treatment compared to TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells.
source: However, WT RAW264.7 cells exhibited a sustained and much higher degree of detectable Caspase-3 after prolonged etoposide treatment for 16 and 24 hr, which was highly significant at 16 hr (Figure 7A and B; numerical values Figure 7—source data 1), suggesting that TFE3 and TFEB are critical for the proper induction of DNA damage induced apoptosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and B with statistical analysis.

claim: After 16 and 24 hr etoposide treatment, significantly more TFEB/TFE3 DKO RAW264.7 cells are live compared to WT cells.
source: After 16 and 24 hr etoposide treatment, major differences in cell viability were observed with significantly more live TFEB/TFE3 DKO compared to RAW264.7 WT cells as evidenced by the number of AnnexinV-/7-AAD- cells detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental flow cytometry data from Annexin V/7-AAD assay.

claim: WT RAW264.7 cells show a significant increase in early and late apoptotic cells compared to TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells at 16 hr and 24 hr etoposide treatment.
source: This is paralleled with a significant increase in the number of Annexin V+/7-AAD- (early apoptotic) and/or Annexin V+/7-AAD+ (late apoptotic) in WT RAW264.7 cells compared to TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells at 16 hr and 24 hr etoposide treatment, respectively (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Close to 5000 genes are differentially expressed between etoposide-treated WT and TFEB/TFE3-DKO RAW264.7 cells.
source: The comparative transcriptome analysis between etoposide-treated WT and TFEB/TFE3-DKO RAW264.7 cells revealed that close to 5000 genes were differentially express between both cell lines (Figure 8A and B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Gene ontology analysis shows a very strong down-regulation of genes implicated in response to DNA damage and DNA repair in TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis of 'Biological Process' terms showed a very strong down-regulation of genes implicated in response to DNA damage and DNA repair (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The most significantly downregulated GO categories in TFEB/TFE3 DKO cells are those related to mitosis.
source: More surprising was the significant downregulation of genes implicated in cell cycle regulation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A). In fact, the most significantly downregulated categories were those related to mitosis, including 'M phase', 'M phase of mitotic cell cycle', 'nuclear division', 'mitosis', 'organelle fission', 'chromosome segregation', 'mitotic cell cycle' and 'cell division'.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 91% of genes regulated by the DREAM pathway show more significant downregulation in TFEB/TFE3 DKO than in WT cells following etoposide treatment.
source: As seen in Figure 8, no major differences were observed in the expression of cell cycle regulators between WT and DKOs under control conditions (Figure 8C, Supplementary file 3). In contrast, 91% (240 out of 262) of the genes regulated by the DREAM pathway showed a much more significant downregulation in TFEB/TFE3 DKO than in WT cells following etoposide treatment (Figure 8C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 8C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: ChIP-seq analysis shows increased TFE3 binding to the promoter of CDK4 and CDK7 following TFE3 activation.
source: Interestingly, we observed increased TFE3 binding to the promoter of CDK4 and CDK7 following TFE3 activation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Over-expression of TFEB or TFE3 results in a significant increase in CDK4 and CDK7 mRNA and protein levels.
source: As seen in Figure 9B–C; numerical values Figure 9—source datas 1 and 2, over-expression of either TFEB or TFE3 resulted in a significant increase in CDK4 and CDK7 mRNA and protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 9B–C.

claim: Phosphorylation of Rb is significantly reduced in TFEB/TEF3 DKO cells.
source: Furthermore, phosphorylation of Rb, a CDK4 target, was significantly reduced in TFEB/TEF3 DKO cells (Figure 9D–F; numerical values Figure 9—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 9D–F with statistical analysis.

claim: Reduced RBL2 phosphorylation is observed in TFEB/TFE3-depleted cells.
source: We also observed reduced RBL2 phosphorylation in TFEB/TFE3-depleted cells (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental Western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: DNA damage activates TFE3 and TFEB in a p53 and mTORC1 dependent manner.
source: Here we demonstrate that DNA damage activates TFE3 and TFEB in a p53 and mTORC1 dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript showing p53 and mTORC1 dependence.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis of TFEB/TFE3 double-knockout cells exposed to etoposide reveals a profound dysregulation of the DNA damage response.
source: RNA-Seq analysis of TFEB/TFE3 double-knockout cells exposed to etoposide reveals a profound dysregulation of the DNA damage response, including upstream regulators and downstream p53 targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: TFE3 and TFEB contribute to sustain p53-dependent response by stabilizing p53 protein levels.
source: TFE3 and TFEB contribute to sustain p53-dependent response by stabilizing p53 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing p53 half-life and protein level changes in DKO cells.

claim: In TFEB/TFE3 DKOs, p53 half-life is significantly decreased due to elevated Mdm2 levels.
source: In TFEB/TFE3 DKOs, p53 half-life is significantly decreased due to elevated Mdm2 levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing decreased p53 half-life and elevated Mdm2 in DKO cells.

claim: Transcriptional profiles of genes involved in lysosome membrane permeabilization and cell death pathways are dysregulated in TFEB/TFE3-depleted cells.
source: Transcriptional profiles of genes involved in lysosome membrane permeabilization and cell death pathways are dysregulated in TFEB/TFE3-depleted cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq and qRT-PCR data showing dysregulation of LMP and cell death genes.

claim: Prolonged DNA damage results in impaired LMP and apoptosis induction in TFEB/TFE3-depleted cells.
source: Consequently, prolonged DNA damage results in impaired LMP and apoptosis induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced LMP and apoptosis in DKO cells.

claim: Expression of multiple genes implicated in cell cycle control is altered in TFEB/TFE3 DKOs.
source: Finally, expression of multiple genes implicated in cell cycle control is altered in TFEB/TFE3 DKOs, revealing a previously unrecognized role of TFEB and TFE3 in the regulation of cell cycle checkpoints in response to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data showing altered expression of cell cycle genes.
